title: What is Ramadan?
summary: Ramadan is a special month for Muslims all over the world.

sections.heading: A special month
sections.text: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims all over the world look forward to it every year.

sections.heading: Watching the moon
sections.text: Islamic months follow the moon. A new month begins when the thin crescent moon is seen. That is why Ramadan can have 29 or 30 days. Grown-ups listen for the local announcement to know when it starts.

sections.heading: What do Muslims do?
sections.text: In Ramadan, grown-up Muslims who are healthy fast during the day. People also pray, read the Quran, give to others and try extra hard to be kind.

sections.heading: A month of the Quran
sections.text: Muslims believe the Quran was first sent down to Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the month of Ramadan.

sections.heading: And at the end?
sections.text: When Ramadan finishes, Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr with family, friends and thankful hearts.

keyWords.meaning: The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, the month of fasting.
The thin curved shape of the new moon.

tryThis: With a grown-up, look at the night sky this week. Can you see the moon? What shape is it?
sourceNote: General introduction; reviewer to confirm wording on the start of the month and the revelation of the Quran.

quickCheck.question: Why can Ramadan have 29 or 30 days?
options: Because Islamic months follow the moon
quickCheck.explanation: Islamic months follow the moon. A new month begins when the thin crescent moon is seen.

title: Why do Muslims fast?
summary: Fasting in Ramadan is one of the five pillars of Islam.

sections.heading: What is fasting?
sections.text: Fasting means not eating or drinking from dawn until sunset. In Arabic, fasting is called sawm.

sections.heading: Why do Muslims fast?
sections.text: Fasting in Ramadan is one of the five pillars of Islam. Muslims fast because Allah asks them to. It helps them feel close to Allah, be patient and be thankful.

sections.heading: Remembering others
sections.text: When people feel a little hungry, they remember people who do not have enough food. This helps them want to share and help.

sections.heading: Who fasts?
sections.text: Grown-ups who are healthy fast in Ramadan. Children do not have to fast. Some children practise for part of a day when their family says it is okay. People who are sick do not have to fast.

sections.heading: Your health comes first
sections.text: If you ever feel dizzy, weak or unwell, tell a grown-up straight away. Your Ramadan adventure is special whether or not you are fasting.

keyWords.meaning: The Arabic word for fasting.
Something strong that holds a building up. Islam has five pillars.

tryThis: Ask a grown-up in your family: what do you like most about Ramadan?
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm the reasons given and the summary of who is not required to fast. No rulings beyond the basics are given.

quickCheck.question: What does fasting mean?
options: Not eating or drinking from dawn until sunset
quickCheck.explanation: Fasting means not eating or drinking from dawn until sunset. In Arabic it is called sawm.

title: What is Suhoor?
summary: Suhoor is the meal before dawn.

sections.heading: An early meal
sections.text: Suhoor is the meal people eat before dawn, before a day of fasting begins. It is still dark outside!

sections.heading: Waking up together
sections.text: Families often wake up very early to eat Suhoor together. It can feel cosy and special.

sections.heading: Good food and water
sections.text: Grown-ups try to eat healthy food and drink water at Suhoor. In the Maldives, some families might eat rice, fish, roshi or fruit. Every family is different.

sections.heading: Then comes Fajr
sections.text: After Suhoor, it is time for the dawn prayer, called Fajr.

keyWords.meaning: The meal eaten before dawn in Ramadan.
The time early in the morning when the sky starts to get light.

tryThis: Ask your family what they like to eat at Suhoor.
sourceNote: Basic description of Suhoor; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: When do people eat Suhoor?
options: Before dawn, while it is still dark
quickCheck.explanation: Suhoor is the meal before dawn, before a day of fasting begins.

title: What is Iftar?
summary: Iftar is the meal at sunset that ends the day's fast.

sections.heading: Sunset meal
sections.text: Iftar is the meal at sunset, when the fast for the day ends. Many people listen for the call to the Maghrib prayer.

sections.heading: Dates and water
sections.text: Many Muslims like to begin Iftar with dates and water.

sections.heading: Sharing together
sections.text: Iftar is a happy time. Families share food and sometimes invite neighbours, relatives or friends.

sections.heading: Iftar in the Maldives
sections.text: Some Maldivian families enjoy treats like masroshi, gulha and bajiya, with fruit and drinks. Every family has its own favourites.

keyWords.meaning: The meal at sunset when the fast ends.
The prayer just after sunset.

tryThis: Help set the table for a family meal (with a grown-up nearby).
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm description of Iftar customs.

quickCheck.question: What do many Muslims like to begin Iftar with?
quickCheck.explanation: Many Muslims like to begin Iftar with dates and water.

title: What is the Quran?
summary: The Quran is the holy book of Islam.

sections.heading: The holy book
sections.text: The Quran is the holy book of Islam. Muslims believe it is the word of Allah.

sections.heading: How it came
sections.text: Muslims believe the Quran was sent to Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, through the Angel Jibril, a little at a time, over many years.

sections.heading: In Arabic
sections.text: The Quran is in Arabic. It has 114 chapters. Each chapter is called a surah. Many children learn to read it with a teacher.

sections.heading: With respect
sections.text: Muslims handle the Quran with care. They keep it clean and in a special place. Many people try to read more of it in Ramadan.

keyWords.meaning: The holy book of Islam.
A chapter of the Quran.

tryThis: Ask a grown-up to show you how your family keeps the Quran in a special place.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm. A short verified recitation or surah reference could be added by the reviewer.

quickCheck.question: What is a chapter of the Quran called?
quickCheck.explanation: The Quran has 114 chapters, and each chapter is called a surah.

title: What is Salah?
summary: Salah is the prayer Muslims pray five times a day.

sections.heading: Talking to Allah
sections.text: Salah is the special prayer Muslims pray five times every day. It is one of the five pillars of Islam.

sections.heading: Five prayers
sections.text: The five prayers are Fajr at dawn, Dhuhr after midday, Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib after sunset and Isha at night.

sections.heading: Getting ready
sections.text: Before praying, Muslims wash in a special way called wudu. They face the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah.

sections.heading: In Ramadan
sections.text: Many Muslims also go to special night prayers in Ramadan called Taraweeh. Children often learn to pray by watching and joining their family.

keyWords.meaning: The prayer Muslims pray five times a day.
Washing in a special way before prayer.

tryThis: Can you name the five prayers? Say them to a grown-up.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm names and times of prayers. No prayer times are shown in the app.

quickCheck.question: How many times a day do Muslims pray Salah?
quickCheck.explanation: Muslims pray five times a day: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha.

title: The Five Pillars of Islam
summary: Five important practices that hold up a Muslim's life, like pillars hold up a building.

sections.heading: Strong pillars
sections.text: Pillars hold up a building. Islam has five pillars that are very important to Muslims.

sections.heading: 1. Shahada
sections.text: Believing and saying that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His messenger.

sections.heading: 2. Salah
sections.text: Praying five times every day.

sections.heading: 3. Zakat
sections.text: Giving part of your money to help people in need, for grown-ups who have enough.

sections.heading: 4. Sawm
sections.text: Fasting in the month of Ramadan, for grown-ups who are able.

sections.heading: 5. Hajj
sections.text: Visiting Makkah for the pilgrimage once in a lifetime, for grown-ups who are able.

keyWords.meaning: The declaration of faith.
The pilgrimage to Makkah.

tryThis: Hold up one finger for each pillar and say its name.
sourceNote: Standard summary of the five pillars; reviewer to confirm wording of the Shahada summary.

quickCheck.question: Which of these is one of the five pillars of Islam?
quickCheck.explanation: The five pillars are Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm and Hajj.

title: What is charity?
summary: Charity means giving to help others.

sections.heading: Giving to help
sections.text: Charity means giving something to help others, like food, money, clothes or your time.

sections.heading: Sadaqah
sections.text: In Islam, giving you choose to do is called sadaqah. It can be big or small.

sections.heading: In Ramadan
sections.text: Many Muslims try to give more in Ramadan. Families might share food, give to people in need or help their community.

sections.heading: You can help too
sections.text: With a grown-up, you might choose a book or toy in good condition to give, or help prepare food to share.

keyWords.meaning: Giving to help people who need it.
Giving that you choose to do.

tryThis: With a grown-up, find one thing you could share or give.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm the explanation of sadaqah.

quickCheck.question: What is giving you choose to do called in Islam?
quickCheck.explanation: Giving you choose to do is called sadaqah. It can be big or small.

title: What is Zakat?
summary: Zakat is a special kind of giving and one of the five pillars.

sections.heading: A pillar of Islam
sections.text: Zakat is one of the five pillars of Islam. Grown-ups who have enough money give a part of it to help people in need.

sections.heading: Sharing what we have
sections.text: Zakat reminds Muslims that everything they have is a gift from Allah, and that it is good to share.

sections.heading: Before Eid
sections.text: At the end of Ramadan, families also give a special charity called Zakat al-Fitr, so that everyone can enjoy Eid.

sections.heading: Grown-ups take care of it
sections.text: Grown-ups work out and give Zakat. Children can learn about it and help their family be generous.

keyWords.meaning: Giving part of your money to people in need, a pillar of Islam.
A special charity given before Eid al-Fitr.

tryThis: Ask a grown-up how your family helps people in need.
sourceNote: Simplified; reviewer to confirm. No amounts or calculations are given.

quickCheck.question: What special charity do families give at the end of Ramadan?
quickCheck.explanation: Families give Zakat al-Fitr so that everyone can enjoy Eid.

title: What is a dua?
summary: A dua is when we ask Allah for something, in our own words.

sections.heading: Talking to Allah
sections.text: A dua is when a person asks Allah for help, says thank you or asks for good things. You can make a dua at any time.

sections.heading: Any language
sections.text: You can make a dua in your own words and in any language. Many people raise their hands when they make a dua.

sections.heading: Duas you may hear
sections.text: Many Muslims say "Bismillah", which means "In the name of Allah", before eating. Your family may teach you other duas too.

sections.heading: Kind duas
sections.text: You can make a dua for your family, your friends and people who need help.

keyWords.meaning: Asking Allah for something in your own words.
In the name of Allah.

tryThis: Ask a grown-up to teach you a dua your family likes to say.
sourceNote: Reviewer to verify the meaning given for "Bismillah". Specific dua texts are deliberately left to families/reviewer.

quickCheck.question: In which language can you make a dua?
options: In any language, in your own words
quickCheck.explanation: You can make a dua in your own words and in any language, at any time.

title: What is a mosque?
summary: A mosque is a place where Muslims pray together.

sections.heading: A place to pray
sections.text: A mosque is a building where Muslims pray together. In Arabic it is called a masjid.

sections.heading: What will I see?
sections.text: Many mosques have a dome and a tall tower called a minaret. Inside there is a lot of space for people to pray in rows.

sections.heading: The call to prayer
sections.text: The adhan is the call to prayer. It lets people know it is time to pray.

sections.heading: Mosque manners
sections.text: At a mosque, we take off our shoes, keep clean, use a quiet voice and walk calmly.

sections.heading: Mosques in the Maldives
sections.text: There are mosques on many islands in the Maldives. Families often go together on Fridays.

keyWords.meaning: The Arabic word for mosque.
The call to prayer.

tryThis: Next time you visit a mosque with your family, put your shoes neatly in place.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm. The village mosque in the app is a fictional design, not a real building.

quickCheck.question: What is the call to prayer called?
quickCheck.explanation: The adhan is the call to prayer. It lets people know it is time to pray.

title: Good manners
summary: Islam teaches us to be polite and kind to everyone.

sections.heading: Greeting with peace
sections.text: Muslims greet each other by saying "Assalamu alaikum", which means "Peace be upon you". The reply is "Wa alaikum assalam".

sections.heading: Please and thank you
sections.text: Saying please and thank you shows we care about other people.

sections.heading: At mealtimes
sections.text: Many Muslim families say Bismillah before eating, eat with their right hand and do not waste food.

sections.heading: Listening
sections.text: Good manners also means listening when someone is talking and waiting for your turn.

keyWords.meaning: Peace be upon you.
Polite and kind ways of behaving.

tryThis: Greet each person in your family with salaam today.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm greeting translation and mealtime manners.

quickCheck.question: What is the reply to "Assalamu alaikum"?
quickCheck.explanation: "Assalamu alaikum" means "Peace be upon you". The reply is "Wa alaikum assalam".

title: Honesty
summary: Being honest means telling the truth.

sections.heading: Telling the truth
sections.text: Being honest means telling the truth, even when it is hard. Islam teaches that honesty is very important.

sections.heading: Keeping promises
sections.text: Honest people keep their promises. If you say you will help, try your best to do it.

sections.heading: Giving things back
sections.text: If you find something that is not yours, give it to a grown-up so it can go back to its owner.

sections.heading: It's okay to make mistakes
sections.text: Everyone makes mistakes. Saying "I did it, I'm sorry" is brave and honest.

keyWords.meaning: Telling the truth.

tryThis: Think of a time someone was honest with you. How did it feel?
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: You find a toy that is not yours. What is the honest thing to do?
options: Give it to a grown-up so it can go back to its owner
quickCheck.explanation: Give it to a grown-up so it can go back to its owner.

title: Patience
summary: Patience means waiting calmly and not giving up.

sections.heading: What is patience?
sections.text: Patience means waiting calmly, even when it is hard. In Arabic it is called sabr.

sections.heading: Patience in Ramadan
sections.text: In Ramadan, grown-ups who fast practise patience. Everyone can practise patience by waiting their turn and staying calm.

sections.heading: When things are hard
sections.text: When something is difficult, you can take a deep breath, ask for help and try again.

sections.heading: Little by little
sections.text: Patience grows little by little, like a seed growing into a palm tree.

keyWords.meaning: The Arabic word for patience.

tryThis: Next time you have to wait, take three slow breaths.
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: What is patience called in Arabic?
quickCheck.explanation: Patience is called sabr. It means waiting calmly, even when it is hard.

title: Gratitude
summary: Gratitude means being thankful.

sections.heading: Being thankful
sections.text: Gratitude means being thankful for the good things we have. In Arabic it is called shukr.

sections.heading: Alhamdulillah
sections.text: Muslims say "Alhamdulillah", which means "All praise is for Allah", to thank Allah.

sections.heading: Thanking people
sections.text: We can also thank the people who help us, like our family, teachers and friends.

sections.heading: Little things
sections.text: We can be thankful for little things too: a cool drink, a smile, the sea and the stars.

keyWords.meaning: Being thankful.
All praise is for Allah.

tryThis: Name three things you are thankful for today.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm translation of Alhamdulillah.

quickCheck.question: What does "Alhamdulillah" mean?
quickCheck.explanation: Muslims say "Alhamdulillah", which means "All praise is for Allah", to thank Allah.

title: Helping neighbours
summary: Islam teaches us to be kind to our neighbours.

sections.heading: Who are our neighbours?
sections.text: Neighbours are the people who live near us. Islam teaches that we should be kind to our neighbours.

sections.heading: Kind things to do
sections.text: We can smile and greet them, keep our street clean and share with them.

sections.heading: Sharing in Ramadan
sections.text: Many families share plates of food with neighbours in Ramadan. Always ask a grown-up first and go together.

keyWords.meaning: Someone who lives near you.

tryThis: With a grown-up, think of one kind thing your family could do for a neighbour.
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: Before sharing food with a neighbour, what should you do?
options: Ask a grown-up first and go together
quickCheck.explanation: Always ask a grown-up first and go together.

title: Laylatul Qadr
summary: A very special night in the last part of Ramadan.

sections.heading: The Night of Power
sections.text: Laylatul Qadr means the Night of Power. Muslims believe it is a very special and blessed night.

sections.heading: When is it?
sections.text: Muslims believe it is one of the last ten nights of Ramadan. Nobody knows for sure which night it is.

sections.heading: What do people do?
sections.text: Many Muslims pray, read the Quran and make dua in the last ten nights, hoping to find this special night.

sections.heading: A night to remember
sections.text: Muslims believe the Quran was first revealed on this night.

keyWords.meaning: The Night of Power, a special night in Ramadan.

tryThis: With your family, make a dua for the people you love.
sourceNote: Learning theme only — the app never claims which night it is. Reviewer may add a verified reference.

quickCheck.question: When is Laylatul Qadr?
options: On the first night of Ramadan
One of the last ten nights of Ramadan
quickCheck.explanation: Muslims believe it is one of the last ten nights of Ramadan. Nobody knows for sure which night it is.

title: Eid al-Fitr
summary: The happy celebration at the end of Ramadan.

sections.heading: Celebrating together
sections.text: Eid al-Fitr is the celebration at the end of Ramadan. It is the first day of the next month, Shawwal.

sections.heading: When does it start?
sections.text: Like Ramadan, Eid starts when the new crescent moon is seen. Grown-ups listen for the local announcement.

sections.heading: Eid morning
sections.text: On Eid morning, many Muslims wear clean or new clothes and go to the special Eid prayer.

sections.heading: Eid Mubarak!
sections.text: People greet each other with "Eid Mubarak", which means "Blessed Eid". Families visit each other and share food.

sections.heading: In the Maldives
sections.text: In the Maldives, many people call Eid al-Fitr "Kuda Eid". Every family celebrates in its own way.

keyWords.meaning: The celebration at the end of Ramadan.
Blessed Eid — a happy Eid greeting.

tryThis: Make an Eid card for someone in your family.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm, including the local name Kuda Eid.

quickCheck.question: What do many people in the Maldives call Eid al-Fitr?
quickCheck.explanation: In the Maldives, many people call Eid al-Fitr "Kuda Eid".

title: Sharing and generosity
summary: Being generous means happily sharing what we have.

sections.heading: What is generosity?
sections.text: Being generous means happily giving and sharing with others.

sections.heading: Small things count
sections.text: Sharing does not have to be big. You can share a snack, a toy, a turn or a smile.

sections.heading: Sharing in Ramadan
sections.text: In Ramadan, many families share food with others and give to people in need.

keyWords.meaning: Happy to give and share.

tryThis: Share something with someone today.
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: Which of these is a way to share?
options: Sharing a snack, a toy or a turn
quickCheck.explanation: Sharing does not have to be big. You can share a snack, a toy, a turn or a smile.

title: Caring for family and community
summary: Islam teaches us to care for our family and the people around us.

sections.heading: Family first
sections.text: Islam teaches us to be kind and respectful to our parents and family.

sections.heading: Helping at home
sections.text: You can help at home by tidying up, setting the table or helping a younger brother or sister.

sections.heading: Our community
sections.text: Our community is everyone around us. People help each other, like keeping beaches and streets clean.

keyWords.meaning: The people who live and work around us.

tryThis: Ask someone in your family: how can I help you today?
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: Which is a way to help at home?
quickCheck.explanation: You can help at home by tidying up, setting the table or helping a younger brother or sister.

title: Cleanliness
summary: Islam teaches Muslims to keep clean and tidy.

sections.heading: Keeping clean
sections.text: Islam teaches that keeping clean is very important. Muslims wash before prayer with wudu.

sections.heading: Clean places
sections.text: We keep our homes, mosques, beaches and streets clean.

sections.heading: You can help
sections.text: Put rubbish in the bin, tidy your toys and wash your hands before eating.

keyWords.meaning: Washing in a special way before prayer.

tryThis: Tidy one small space in your room.
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: How do Muslims wash before prayer?
quickCheck.explanation: Muslims wash in a special way called wudu before prayer.

title: Good words
summary: Kind words can make someone's whole day better.

sections.heading: Words are powerful
sections.text: Our words can make people feel happy or sad. Islam teaches us to say good and kind words.

sections.heading: Kind things to say
sections.text: "Well done!" "Can I help?" "Thank you!" "You can do it!"

sections.heading: If we can't say something kind
sections.text: Sometimes it is better to stay quiet than to say something unkind.

keyWords.meaning: To give someone hope and help them keep going.

tryThis: Say something encouraging to someone today.
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: Which of these are kind words?
quickCheck.explanation: Kind words like "Can I help?" and "Well done!" can make people feel happy.

title: Forgiveness
summary: Forgiving means letting go of being upset with someone.

sections.heading: What is forgiveness?
sections.text: Forgiving someone means you stop being cross with them after they say sorry.

sections.heading: Allah is forgiving
sections.text: Muslims believe Allah is the Most Forgiving. Muslims ask Allah to forgive them, and try to forgive others too.

sections.heading: Saying sorry
sections.text: When we make a mistake, we can say sorry and try to make things better.

keyWords.meaning: To stop being upset with someone.

tryThis: If you had a quarrel with someone, try to make up today.
sourceNote: Reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: What can we do when we make a mistake?
options: Say sorry and try to make things better
quickCheck.explanation: When we make a mistake, we can say sorry and try to make things better.

title: Respect for parents and elders
summary: Showing respect means treating people kindly and politely.

sections.heading: Respecting parents
sections.text: Islam teaches us to be kind and respectful to our parents.

sections.heading: Respecting elders
sections.text: We greet older people, speak politely to them and listen to them.

sections.heading: Ways to show respect
sections.text: Offer your seat, help carry something light, and say thank you.

keyWords.meaning: Treating someone kindly and politely.

tryThis: Greet an older person in your family with salaam and a smile.
sourceNote: Values lesson; reviewer to confirm.

quickCheck.question: Which is a way to show respect to elders?
quickCheck.explanation: We can offer our seat, help carry something light and say thank you.
